Dear Dr. Vance,

Thank you for seeing this 45-year-old gentleman who presented to our outpatient service for a cardiovascular screening ahead of an upcoming charity race. He is currently asymptomatic, works as an administrator, is a non-smoker, and takes no prescription medications.

His resting 12-lead electrocardiogram revealed an rSr' morphology in the right precordial leads consistent with a partial right bundle branch delay, accompanied by prominent, persistent upward shifting of the ST segments in leads V1 and V2. Because of these findings, a 48-hour ambulatory monitor was arranged, which captured several short, asymptomatic runs of broad-complex ventricular tachyarrhythmia.

On direct questioning, he denies any fainting episodes, near-blackouts, or transient loss of consciousness. He has had no sensations of rapid heart fluttering or skipped beats. He has never suffered a circulatory arrest, and his family history is entirely negative for instances of sudden unexpected demise in young relatives. 

Physical examination was unremarkable, with a resting blood pressure of 122/76 mmHg and clear heart sounds without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Basic laboratory evaluations, including serum electrolytes and routine chemistries, were entirely normal. His repolarization parameters were likewise preserved, showing a corrected QT measurement well within reference limits without any lengthening.

Given these electrical anomalies, I would appreciate your expert electrophysiology assessment and advice regarding further risk stratification.

Sincerely,

Dr. Arthur Miller
